name: Canary Deployments
intent: Send a new version to a small share of real traffic, compare it with the stable version, and widen or roll back automatically based on what the numbers say.
scenario: The checkout service releases v2, which has a latent bug that makes about 2% of requests fail (v1 fails about 1%). Staging never showed it. A router sends 5% of traffic to v2, a health gate compares the two versions' error rates, and widening or rolling back is decided by that comparison instead of by someone watching a dashboard.
problem: Tests and staging cannot reproduce production: real data, real traffic mixes and real dependencies expose bugs only after release. Shipping to everyone at once means every user hits the bug before anyone notices, and noticing takes minutes or hours. You want production to be the test, but with a small blast radius, a decision rule that does not depend on someone staring at graphs, and a fast way back.

howItWorks.title: Run v2 beside v1 and split traffic by weight
howItWorks.text: v2 is deployed as a separate, small set of instances next to the stable fleet. A load balancer, service mesh or ingress sends a weighted share of requests to it, for example 5%. Prefer sticky routing (hash of user or session) so one user does not bounce between versions mid-checkout, and so the canary's data stays clean.

howItWorks.title: Bake: collect the same metrics from both versions
howItWorks.text: The canary stays at its share for a bake time, long enough to gather a useful sample and to cover slow effects such as caches warming or a memory leak. A request-count minimum matters more than the clock: 5 minutes at 1% of a quiet service may be 30 requests, which tells you almost nothing.

howItWorks.title: Health gate: compare canary against stable, not against a fixed number
howItWorks.text: The gate compares the canary's error rate and latency (p95 or p99) with the stable version measured at the same time, so a bad dependency or a traffic spike hits both and cancels out. It asks whether the difference is bigger than random noise: for error counts, roughly how many standard deviations above what the stable rate predicts. Typical thresholds are 2 to 4 standard deviations, plus an absolute floor so tiny differences never trigger.

howItWorks.title: Decide: promote, hold or roll back
howItWorks.text: Not enough data means hold (keep baking), not pass. A clear regression means roll back immediately: set the canary weight to 0 and the stable fleet carries on untouched. A clean bake means widen to the next stage, commonly 1%, 5%, 25%, 50%, 100%. The decision is automatic so it happens at 3 a.m. as reliably as at 3 p.m.

howItWorks.title: Widen in stages, then retire v1
howItWorks.text: Each stage repeats the bake and gate with a bigger sample, so small effects that were invisible at 5% become visible at 25%. When the last stage passes, v2 takes all traffic. Keep v1 ready for a while, because the fastest rollback is changing a weight back.

pros: Limits the blast radius: a bug reaches 5% of users for a few minutes, not 100% for an hour
Tests against real production traffic, data and dependencies
Automated gates remove the need for a person to watch the release
Rollback is just a weight change, with v1 still running
cons: Needs good metrics per version and enough traffic for the comparison to mean something
Small samples mislead: low traffic or a low share gives false alarms and missed bugs
Two versions run at once, so schema changes and APIs must be compatible with both
Slower than a big-bang release, and the pipeline (routing, metrics, gate) is real work to build
whenToUse: User-facing services with enough traffic to measure a difference within minutes
Changes whose risk only shows under real load or data (new queries, dependency upgrades, rewrites)
Teams that release often and want rollback to be a non-event
whenNotToUse: Very low traffic: a few requests a minute cannot be compared statistically, so use blue-green with a smoke test instead
Changes that cannot run side by side, such as incompatible database migrations or one-shot batch jobs
Bugs that only show up in rare, high-value paths the canary share seldom exercises, unless you route those paths on purpose
pitfalls: Comparing the canary to a fixed threshold (error rate under 2%) instead of to the stable version at the same time, so a bad dependency day fails every release
Judging on a handful of requests: 3 errors out of 60 can be pure noise, and 0 errors out of 60 proves nothing
Peeking at the gate every minute with a loose threshold, which multiplies the chance of a false alarm; require a minimum sample and a sensible threshold
Only watching errors: a version that is 3 times slower or leaks memory passes an error-rate gate
Non-sticky routing, so one user sees both versions and caches, sessions or A/B tests get mixed up
Forgetting that rolling back code does not undo what the canary already wrote (bad data, sent emails)

roles.label: Users
roles.description: Checkout requests arriving at about 1000 per minute.

roles.label: Traffic splitter
roles.description: A load balancer or mesh that sends a weighted share of requests to each version.

roles.label: Stable v1
roles.description: The current version, the baseline everything is compared with.

roles.label: Canary v2
roles.description: The new version, running on a few instances with a small share of traffic.

roles.label: Health gate
roles.description: Compares canary and stable metrics and decides to hold, widen or roll back.
